vignette:
Mika is a 45-year-old American man of Pacific Islander background, a divorced chef who has spent most of his adult life defining himself by stamina, precision, and the ability to command a kitchen under pressure. Before the assault, he thought of himself as someone who could handle anything: long shifts on his feet, the heat and noise of dinner service, the relentless pace of restaurant work. What happened to him has become something he can speak about plainly in words, but not in a way that feels settled. He can say that he was raped. He can tell another person where it happened, who did it, and that he did not consent. Yet when he tries to stay with the memory for more than a few moments, it breaks apart on him.

The assault happened after a late shift, when he was exhausted and still carrying the physical strain of service in his body. The details he gives are strikingly direct at first, almost matter-of-fact, as if he has learned to state the facts quickly before something in him shuts down. He remembers the immediate recognition that he was in danger and the humiliating intimacy of what was done to him. What remains hardest is not naming it but holding onto the whole sequence. He will begin telling it in order, then stop, frown, and correct himself, uncertain what came first and what followed. He knows there are pieces missing. He has the sense of reaching toward the memory and then abruptly shoving it away before it is complete, as though finishing it would expose him to something unbearable. In session he has said that he can talk about it “very easily,” and this is true in a narrow sense; he does not go mute or avoid the basic facts. But as he speaks, the chronology slips, and before the memory can fully form he cuts himself off, changes tense, or says he would rather leave it there.

In the weeks after the rape, Mika found that the meaning of what had happened settled heavily into how he saw himself. He had always taken pride in being capable, a man known for endurance and control, and he came to believe that this version of himself was gone. In the kitchen, where he used to move with certainty from station to station, he began to feel as though the qualities that had defined him had been stripped out of him. Even on ordinary shifts, tying his apron and stepping onto the line could bring a sense of fraudulence: other people still saw a seasoned chef, while he felt like someone ruined and diminished, no longer able to be the person he had spent decades becoming.

Alongside this, he described a persistent feeling of contamination that attached not only to his body but to daily routines. The physical labor of cooking placed him in constant contact with his hands, skin, sweat, and clothing, and this made the feeling hard to escape. There were days in the restaurant when a smear of sauce on his jacket or the damp heat of the kitchen would abruptly fill him with disgust, not because of the stain itself but because it seemed to echo the sense that something unclean had been left on him by the assault. He would go home after service and stand under the shower longer than he intended, not with any clear expectation that it would fix anything, but because he could not shake the conviction that he was dirty in a way ordinary washing could not reach.

Over the following months, these beliefs reshaped the story he told himself about his life. The divorce had already left him feeling solitary, and after the rape he increasingly concluded that what happened had destroyed what was left. He did not describe this as a temporary setback. To him it felt final. The restaurant had once been the central place where he felt skilled and respected; now it had become a daily reminder of the man he believed he was no longer capable of being. He continued working, but the sense of competence that had organized his identity was gone. He saw his future narrowing around the assault, as if every part of his life had to be understood in relation to it.

By the time he sought help, Mika was exhausted by the effort of carrying a memory he could name but not fully hold, and by the weight of conclusions that had begun to feel absolute. What finally brought him in was not a single crisis so much as the realization that he was living as though the rape had already decided the rest of his life. He said he was tired of feeling contaminated, tired of starting to tell himself what happened and then forcing the memory back down, tired of standing in his own kitchen at work and feeling that the person everyone relied on no longer existed. What frightened him most was that he might be right—that his life had in fact been destroyed, and that the capable man he used to be was gone for good. What he hoped, though he said it cautiously, was that talking might help him find some way to live without that conclusion swallowing everything.
